Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] wp2shell SQLi via author__not_in REST parameter (CVE-2026-60137) · [LLM] WordPress web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (wp2shell RCE)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious PHP plugin/webshell dropped in wp-content by web server (wp2shell)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
wp2shell SQLi via author__not_in REST parameter (CVE-2026-60137) AIExploitation High
Hunts WordPress REST requests where the author__not_in parameter (normally an integer ID array) carries SQL-injection content, the core signature of CVE-2026-60137 exploited through the batch-route desync in the wp2shell chain. Targets the initial unauthenticated exploitation step against /wp-json/wp/v2/posts. Rationale: author__not_in is documented (Rapid7/VulnCheck) to accept only integer author IDs; any SQL metacharacter in it is the CVE-2026-60137 injection signature. Note: PoCs delivered inside a POST /wp-json/batch/v1 body won't appear in access-log query strings — pair with WAF body inspection (CommonSecurityLog RequestURL/DeviceCustomString) to catch batch-wrapped payloads. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch left empty: WordPress web-request telemetry does not live in EDR/CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.tenable.com/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137-frequently-asked-questions-about-remote-code-execution • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/wp2shell • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/wp2shell-millions-wordpress-sites-remote-takeover
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (WPScan, Nessus, Qualys) sending SQLi test strings to /wp-json/wp/v2/posts
  • Security researchers / bug-bounty testers replaying the public wp2shell PoC against your own estate
  • Legitimate REST clients that URL-encode a comma-separated author list where an ID happens to contain a matched token (rare)
  • WAF-decoded double requests logging both the encoded and decoded query, doubling alert volume
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("WPScan","Nessus","Qualys","Nuclei","sqlmap") and cIP !in ("<your_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull all requests from the source IP; confirm author__not_in carries SQL (quotes, UNION, SLEEP, information_schema) rather than integers, and note HTTP status — a 200 on a time-based/UNION probe indicates successful injection. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm the site is on WordPress 7.0.2 / 6.9.5 / 6.8.6; if unpatched, force the emergency update immediately (WordPress.org enabled forced auto-updates for this). 3) HUNT: Pivot to the same host for post-exploit activity — new administrator accounts, PHP files written under wp-content/plugins or wp-content/uploads, and web-server/PHP processes spawning shells (see companion UCs).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csUriStem has "wp-json" or csUriQuery has "rest_route"
| where csUriQuery has "author__not_in"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("'","%27","union","select","sleep","information_schema","0x","--","/*")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, Computer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WordPress web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (wp2shell RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects the code-execution stage of wp2shell where the web-request handler (php-fpm, php-cgi, w3wp, apache/nginx) spawns a command shell or download utility — behaviour a normal WordPress worker never exhibits. Confirms the SQLi chain has reached remote code execution. Rationale: The wp2shell chain culminates in uploading a malicious plugin for code execution; that code runs under the PHP/web-server process, so a web worker spawning cmd/sh/whoami/curl is a direct RCE confirmation. Datadog uses windows.sysmon (IIS/PHP-on-Windows); Linux hosts should use source:linux.auditd EXECVE with the same process names. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://cyberinsider.com/wordpress-releases-emergency-update-for-critical-wp2shell-rce-flaw/ • https://www.indusface.com/blog/wp2shell-wordpress-cve-2026-60137-63030-rce/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup plugins (UpdraftPlus, BackWPup) shelling out to mysqldump/gzip/tar
  • Image-optimisation plugins invoking imagemagick 'convert' or 'jpegoptim' via PHP exec()
  • wp-cron running PHP CLI jobs that legitimately call curl to fetch feed data
  • Server-monitoring agents that fork sh from the PHP-FPM pool for health checks
  • Composer/WP-CLI maintenance run interactively on the web host by an admin
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("sh","bash") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("mysqldump","imagemagick","convert","jpegoptim","wp-cron.php","backwpup","updraft"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — reconnaissance (whoami, id, uname), outbound fetch (curl/wget to an unknown host), or an interactive shell are strong TP signals; confirm the parent PHP worker is serving the WordPress vhost. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate WordPress DB and admin credentials; take a forensic copy of wp-content before remediation. 3) HUNT: Enumerate all administrator accounts for rogue additions, list recently-modified PHP files under wp-content/plugins and wp-content/uploads, and review web logs for the preceding author__not_in / batch/v1 exploitation requests.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","httpd","apache2","nginx.exe","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","sh","bash","dash","whoami.exe","whoami","curl.exe","curl","wget","python.exe","python3")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-cgi","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell","pwsh","/sh","/bash","/dash","whoami","curl","wget","python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious PHP plugin/webshell dropped in wp-content by web server (wp2shell) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts PHP files written into wp-content/plugins or wp-content/uploads by the web-server/PHP process — the persistence/execution payload the wp2shell chain uploads after minting a rogue admin. Distinguishes attacker-dropped web shells from normal user-initiated plugin installs by anchoring on the writing process and target path. Rationale: The documented wp2shell escalation uploads a malicious plugin for code execution; a PHP file written into wp-content/plugins or the uploads dir by the PHP/web-server process is the on-disk artefact of that step. Anchored on both the target path and writing process to separate attacker drops from normal user-driven plugin installs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2026-63030-wp2shell-a-critical-remote-code-execution-vulnerability-in-wordpress-core/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/wp2shell • https://www.tenable.com/blog/wp2shell-cve-2026-63030-cve-2026-60137-frequently-asked-questions-about-remote-code-execution
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1505
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator installing or updating a legitimate plugin from the WordPress dashboard (writes many .php files to wp-content/plugins)
  • Automatic plugin/theme auto-updates writing PHP during maintenance windows
  • Caching plugins (W3 Total Cache, WP Rocket) generating advanced-cache.php or object-cache.php
  • Media/gallery plugins writing helper PHP into wp-content/uploads
  • WP-CLI 'wp plugin install' run by an operator on the host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp plugin install","wp plugin update","advanced-cache.php","object-cache.php") or FolderPath has_any ("w3-total-cache","wp-rocket"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the dropped PHP — short obfuscated files or those containing eval/base64_decode/system/assert/$_POST[ are web shells; a single .php landing directly in wp-content/uploads is almost never legitimate. Check whether the write coincides with a dashboard plugin install by a known admin. 2) CONTAIN: Quarantine the file, hash and submit it, and isolate the host if it is a web shell; revoke sessions and reset admin/DB credentials. 3) HUNT: Correlate the write time backward to author__not_in/batch/v1 exploitation in web logs and forward to web-server processes spawning shells or outbound C2, and audit wp_users for a rogue administrator created just before the drop.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "wp-content" and (FolderPath has "plugins" or FolderPath has "uploads")
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-cgi.exe","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","httpd","nginx.exe","nginx","apache2")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "wp-content" and (TargetFilePath has "plugins" or TargetFilePath has "uploads")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-cgi","php.exe","php-fpm","w3wp","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Adobe Acrobat Extension Flaw Let Malicious Sites Read WhatsApp Web Data

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 14 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability chain in the Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension that has over 314 million users, which, if exploited, could facilitate a silent hijack of a user's WhatsApp data. The shortcoming has been codenamed HermeticReader by Guardio Labs. It's officially tracked as CVE-2026-48294 (CVSS score: 7.4), with the vulnerability

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension (<=26.5.2.2) present — HermeticReader/CVE-2026-48294 · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] WhatsApp Web DOM exfiltrated via cross-origin form POST (HermeticReader data theft) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Vulnerable Adobe Acrobat Chrome extension (<=26.5.2.2) present — HermeticReader/CVE-2026-48294 AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces hosts where the Adobe Acrobat PDF Chrome extension (ID efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj) is installed at a version at or below 26.5.2.2, which is exploitable by any malicious web page to read cross-origin WhatsApp Web data. Extracts the version from the on-disk extension folder and flags anything older than the patched 26.5.2.3. Rationale: Uses the exact Adobe Acrobat extension ID (efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj) and the concrete patched-version boundary (26.5.2.3) confirmed by Guardio Labs and Adobe PSIRT; the version is parsed straight from the Chrome on-disk extension folder so the hunt flags only truly-vulnerable builds. Cross-checked guard.io/labs, bleepingcomputer, securityweek, socradar. Cross-checked against: • https://guard.io/labs/hermeticreader---the-vulnerability-that-turned-adobe-300m-install-extension-into-a-full-whatsapp-takeover • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/adobe-chrome-extension-flaw-let-sites-access-private-whatsapp-chats/ • https://www.securityweek.com/flaw-in-adobe-extension-with-300m-installs-enabled-whatsapp-data-theft/ • https://socradar.io/blog/adobe-acrobat-whatsapp-flaw-hermeticreader/
ATT&CKT1176.001 T1189
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome auto-updated the extension to 26.5.2.3 but an older version folder was left on disk transiently before cleanup
  • Roaming/synced Chrome profile copies an old extension version folder onto a new host
  • A patched host where the file-event fired historically but the current build is already 26.5.2.3
  • Forensic/EDR tooling reading (not creating) the extension directory generating file-access noise
  • Enterprise-managed forced-install re-provisioning that momentarily stages an older build
Suppression filter
| where ExtVersion != "26.5.2.3"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the extracted ExtVersion is genuinely <=26.5.2.2 and that no newer 26.5.2.3+ folder exists for the same ID on the host (Chrome keeps only the active version after update). 2) CONTAIN: Force the Chrome Web Store update / push extension policy to 26.5.2.3+, or remove-and-reinstall the extension; for high-risk users, temporarily block the extension via ExtensionInstallBlocklist until patched. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (WhatsApp Web cross-origin POST) on the same user/host over the exposure window to check whether the flaw was actually exploited, and confirm WhatsApp Web was in use during that window.
DeviceFileEvents

WhatsApp Web DOM exfiltrated via cross-origin form POST (HermeticReader data theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the wire signature of HermeticReader exploitation: WhatsApp Web itself performs a top-level form-action navigation that POSTs its rendered DOM (chat list, contacts, open conversation) to a non-Meta host. Flags HTTP POST requests whose Referer/Origin is web.whatsapp.com but whose destination is not a WhatsApp/Meta domain — behaviour WhatsApp Web never exhibits normally (it ships no form-action CSP directive, which is what the exploit abuses). Rationale: Anchored on the article's precise mechanism — WhatsApp Web's missing form-action CSP directive causing WhatsApp itself to POST its rendered DOM cross-origin — expressed as POST + Referer web.whatsapp.com + non-Meta destination, a shape WhatsApp Web never produces legitimately. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty because EDR/FDR network telemetry carries no HTTP method or Referer header; this detection requires web-proxy/SWG logs (ASIM ImWebSession / CommonSecurityLog). Cross-checked against: • https://guard.io/labs/hermeticreader---the-vulnerability-that-turned-adobe-300m-install-extension-into-a-full-whatsapp-takeover • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/adobe-chrome-extension-flaw-let-sites-access-private-whatsapp-chats/
ATT&CKT1185 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WhatsApp Web link-preview or telemetry beacon POSTing to a third-party CDN/analytics host
  • A password-manager or productivity browser extension submitting a form while web.whatsapp.com is the active referer
  • Corporate DLP/SSL-inspection proxy rewriting or normalising the Referer header onto an unrelated POST
  • User manually sharing content from WhatsApp Web into another web app in the same tab flow
  • Meta infrastructure served from a domain not in the all/exclusion list (add newly-observed Meta domains to the filter)
Suppression filter
| where not(DstHostname has_any ("whatsapp.com","whatsapp.net","facebook.com","fbcdn.net","meta.com","fb.com","instagram.com","cdninstagram.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the destination host — resolve WHOIS/age, check if it is newly-registered or unseen across the org; a fresh/rare domain receiving a web.whatsapp.com-referred POST is high-confidence exploitation. 2) CONTAIN: Block the destination domain/IP at the proxy, isolate the source host, and force the user's Adobe Acrobat extension to 26.5.2.3+ (or remove it); invalidate the WhatsApp Web session (log out linked devices). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP/user for other web.whatsapp.com-referred POSTs, correlate with UC1 to confirm a vulnerable extension build was present, and sweep the proxy for the same destination host across all users.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where HttpRequestHeaderReferer has "web.whatsapp.com"
| where isnotempty(DstHostname)
| where not(DstHostname has_any ("whatsapp.com","whatsapp.net","facebook.com","fbcdn.net","meta.com","fb.com"))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpStatusCode
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48294")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48294")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:

falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |

    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:

        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'

level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Hackers Exploit Windmill Flaw to Read Arbitrary Server Files Without Authentication

The Hacker News
2026-07-22 17 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A high-severity security flaw impacting open-source developer platform Windmill has come under active exploitation in the wild, per VulnCheck. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-29059 (CVSS score: 7.5), a case of unauthenticated path traversal impacting Windmill's "get_log_file" endpoint ("/api/w/{workspace}/jobs_u/get_log_file/{filename}"). Windmill get_log_file unauthenticated path traversal exploitation (CVE-2026-29059) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to Windmill's 'get_log_file' endpoint carrying directory-traversal sequences used to read arbitrary server files. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact vulnerable path '/api/w/{workspace}/jobs_u/get_log_file/{filename}' plus '../' and encoded variants, covering both direct Windmill endpoints and the Nextcloud proxy path called out by VulnCheck. Rationale: Anchors on the exact CVE-2026-29059 vulnerable path 'jobs_u/get_log_file' plus raw and URL-encoded traversal tokens and the specific target files (/etc/passwd, /proc) that VulnCheck observed in the wild; the endpoint string makes this Windmill-specific rather than a generic traversal template. Cross-checked SentinelOne, OSV and Field Effect confirming endpoint and payloads. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/CVE-2026-29059 • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/active-exploitation-windmill-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei/VulnCheck) probing the get_log_file endpoint from a known scanning subnet
  • Windmill's own UI legitimately fetching job log files (path contains 'jobs_u/get_log_file' but NO traversal tokens — excluded by the traversal clause)
  • Security researchers or internal red team validating patch status against 1.603.3
  • URL-encoded '..' appearing in a legitimate workspace or filename value that is not actually a traversal
  • WAF already blocked the request (EventOutcome=blocked) — still logged but not a successful read
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei" and SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestURL and scStatus/EventOutcome for the SourceIP; a 200/206 to a get_log_file request containing '../' or '/proc/' confirms a successful arbitrary read. Check whether the instance is < 1.603.3. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the WAF/edge, and if patch is missing, take the Windmill instance offline or gate it behind auth; rotate SUPERADMIN_SECRET and any credentials reachable via file read. 3) Hunt: search the same SourceIP for follow-on reads of /proc/1/environ (secret theft) and subsequent authenticated Bearer-token calls to Windmill job/preview APIs indicating superadmin RCE.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "jobs_u/get_log_file"
| where RequestURL has_any ("../", "..%2f", "..%252f", "%2e%2e", "/proc/", "%2fproc%2f", "/etc/passwd", "%2fetc%2fpasswd")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windmill SUPERADMIN_SECRET theft via /proc/1/environ traversal (CVE-2026-29059) AIExploitation High
Hunts the specific escalation step where the Windmill path traversal is aimed at /proc/1/environ (or /proc/self/environ) to read the SUPERADMIN_SECRET environment variable, which is then usable as a Bearer token for superadmin RCE via the job-preview API. Narrower and higher-severity than generic file read because this target is the direct path to full compromise. Rationale: Uses the article's precise credential-theft primitive: reading /proc/1/environ via the get_log_file traversal to obtain SUPERADMIN_SECRET (confirmed by SentinelOne and OSV). Targeting the process environ file makes this a near-zero-FP indicator of secret theft, not just recon. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://osv.dev/vulnerability/CVE-2026-29059
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised pentest/red-team validating the full exploit chain to prove SUPERADMIN_SECRET exposure
  • Vulnerability scanner plugin that specifically reads /proc/1/environ as its PoC check
  • Internal patch-verification tooling replaying the CVE against a staging Windmill
  • A monitoring agent path that coincidentally references 'environ' but not via the get_log_file endpoint (excluded by the endpoint clause)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>") and RequestClientApplication !has "Nuclei"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm a 200/206 response to the get_log_file request containing /proc/1/environ from an external SourceIP — this means SUPERADMIN_SECRET was likely disclosed. 2) Contain: immediately rotate SUPERADMIN_SECRET and any other secrets stored in the Windmill container environment, revoke active superadmin tokens, block the SourceIP, and patch to 1.603.3+. 3) Hunt: review Windmill API logs for Bearer-token authenticated calls (especially job run/preview) from that SourceIP or new IPs after the read timestamp, indicating the stolen secret was used for RCE.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "jobs_u/get_log_file"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/proc/1/environ", "proc%2f1%2fenviron", "/proc/self/environ", "proc%2fself%2fenviron")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Windmill traversal endpoint enumeration / mass file-read scanning (CVE-2026-29059) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts a single source rapidly issuing many distinct get_log_file traversal requests — the enumeration/scanning behaviour VulnCheck saw across ~170 exposed hosts, and the post-exploitation shift from one manual file read to systematic discovery of additional targets. Threshold-based on distinct traversal paths per source in a short window. Rationale: Turns the article's observed scanning at scale (170 hosts, 24 countries) into a per-source velocity signal keyed on the get_log_file traversal path; the distinct-path count separates a probing/enumeration campaign from a one-off manual read. Threshold-based, so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-29059/ • https://fieldeffect.com/blog/active-exploitation-windmill-vulnerability
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1083
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised authenticated vulnerability scanner sweeping many payload variants against the endpoint
  • Load/performance testing that replays log-fetch requests at volume
  • A single CDN/proxy egress IP aggregating many legitimate Windmill users (NAT) — tune threshold or exclude known proxy IPs
  • Bug-bounty researcher fuzzing the endpoint with a wordlist
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<approved-scanner-ips>", "<known-nat-egress-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review sampleTargets for one SourceIP — a spread of system-file paths (/etc/*, /proc/*) with 200 responses confirms active enumeration and successful reads. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the edge/WAF and confirm the instance is patched to 1.603.3+; if reads succeeded, treat secrets/config on the host as exposed. 3) Hunt: pivot on that SourceIP across all internet-facing apps for the same traversal pattern, and check whether any request reached /proc/1/environ (secret theft) or transitioned to authenticated API calls.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "jobs_u/get_log_file"
| where RequestURL has_any ("../", "..%2f", "%2e%2e", "/proc/", "/etc/")
| summarize reqCount=count(), distinctPaths=dcount(RequestURL), sampleTargets=make_set(RequestURL, 20), firstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), lastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where distinctPaths >= 10   // >=10 distinct traversal targets from one source in 10m = enumeration, not a single manual read
| order by reqCount desc

Langflow /api/v1/validate/code unauthenticated RCE requests (CVE-2026-0770) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated POST requests to Langflow's '/api/v1/validate/code' (exec_globals) endpoint — the vector CISA flagged as actively exploited alongside the Windmill flaw. Article-specific via the exact vulnerable endpoint and the observed payloads (id/whoami, /etc/passwd read, AWS-credential and container-metadata theft, wget/curl malware fetch). Rationale: Targets the confirmed CVE-2026-0770 vulnerable endpoint /api/v1/validate/code (SentinelOne, BleepingComputer, THN KEV writeup) — the exec_globals RCE path. POST bodies (containing __import__/subprocess) aren't always in access logs, so this is scoped as a hunting pivot on the endpoint itself; pair with UC5 for confirmed execution. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0770/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-patch-actively-exploited-langflow-rce-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal Langflow users building/validating flows via the UI, which calls /api/v1/validate/code during normal component editing
  • CI/CD or automated flow-import pipelines that validate code blocks
  • Authorised scanner/PoC (0xBlackash / 0xgh057r3c0n GitHub PoCs) testing the endpoint
  • Health-check probes hitting the API path without a malicious body
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<internal-langflow-user-subnets>", "<approved-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: separate external SourceIPs from internal; a POST to /api/v1/validate/code from an untrusted IP against an unauthenticated/internet-facing Langflow (<= 1.4.2) is high priority. Retrieve the request body from WAF/app logs and look for __import__/subprocess/os.system. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, restrict the endpoint behind auth, and if a body confirms code execution assume root-level host compromise — isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC5 (langflow-spawned shell/curl/wget, cloud-metadata access) on the same host to confirm successful RCE and identify what was stolen.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow post-exploitation: cloud-metadata/credential theft and recon via spawned shell (CVE-2026-0770) AIInstallation High
Confirms successful CVE-2026-0770 RCE on the host by detecting Langflow/Python-parented processes running the observed post-exploitation commands: id/whoami recon, reads of /etc/passwd and /proc/self/environ, access to AWS credentials, and SSRF to the 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata endpoint, or wget/curl second-stage downloads. Rationale: Maps the article's Langflow post-exploitation payloads verbatim — id/whoami, /etc/passwd, AWS credentials, container metadata (169.254.169.254), wget/curl second-stage downloads — to a Langflow/Python parent process chain. The 169.254.169.254 + credential-file combination under a Langflow parent is a high-fidelity confirmed-RCE signal. Corroborated by SentinelOne and CISA/BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0770/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-orders-feds-to-patch-actively-exploited-langflow-rce-flaw/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1552.005 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow flows that intentionally shell out (curl/wget to fetch data) as part of a designed component
  • Cloud-init / SSM / instance agents that legitimately query 169.254.169.254 (excluded here by the Langflow/Python parent constraint)
  • Admin or CI running id/whoami/curl during troubleshooting under a python venv unrelated to Langflow
  • A Langflow component performing an authorised outbound HTTP call to an internal API
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "169.254.169.254" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cloud-init","amazon-ssm-agent","cloud-init-per"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain traces to the Langflow service and inspect the child command line — access to 169.254.169.254 or .aws/credentials from a web-app process is almost never benign. Check Langflow version (<= 1.4.2) and internet exposure. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke/rotate any IAM role credentials the instance profile grants (assume IMDS creds are stolen), kill the Langflow process, and block outbound to attacker infrastructure. 3) Hunt: review outbound connections for wget/curl-downloaded second-stage payloads, new persistence (cron, systemd), and use of the stolen cloud credentials in CloudTrail (AssumeRole/GetCallerIdentity from new IPs).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "langflow" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","whoami","nc","ncat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("169.254.169.254","/latest/meta-data",".aws/credentials","/proc/self/environ","/etc/passwd")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "langflow" or ParentProcessName has "langflow" or ParentProcessName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","whoami","nc","ncat")
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("169.254.169.254","/latest/meta-data",".aws/credentials","/proc/self/environ","/etc/passwd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects Langflow/Python-parented shell, download, and recon utilities reading credential files or reaching the cloud metadata endpoint after CVE-2026-0770 RCE.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hackers-exploit-windmill-flaw-to-read.html
  - https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0770/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/28
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1552.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|contains:
      - 'langflow'
      - 'uvicorn'
      - 'gunicorn'
      - 'python'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/id'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/nc'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '169.254.169.254'
      - '/latest/meta-data'
      - '.aws/credentials'
      - '/proc/self/environ'
      - '/etc/passwd'
  condition: selection_parent and (selection_child or selection_cmd)
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:(*169.254.169.254* OR *"/latest/meta-data"* OR *".aws/credentials"* OR *"/proc/self/environ"* OR *"/etc/passwd"*) OR @process.name:(id OR whoami OR curl OR wget OR nc OR ncat))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(langflow|python3?|uvicorn|gunicorn)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|id|whoami|nc|ncat)$/i OR CommandLine=/169\.254\.169\.254|\/latest\/meta-data|\.aws\/credentials|\/proc\/self\/environ|\/etc\/passwd/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name="*langflow*" OR Endpoint.Processes.parent_process="*langflow*" OR Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")) (Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","whoami","nc","ncat") OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*169.254.169.254*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*/latest/meta-data*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*.aws/credentials*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*/proc/self/environ*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*/etc/passwd*") by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.user Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name="*langflow*" OR Endpoint.Processes.parent_process="*langflow*" OR Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")) (Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","id","whoami","nc","ncat") OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*169.254.169.254*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*/latest/meta-data*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*.aws/credentials*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*/proc/self/environ*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*/etc/passwd*") by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.user Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    product: windows
detection:

            - '\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'

falsepositives:

    where (Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\*"
        OR Registry.registry_path="*\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\*")

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-29059", "CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030", "CVE-2021-27137", "CVE-2026-0770")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-29059", "CVE-2026-60137", "CVE-2026-63030", "CVE-2021-27137", "CVE-2026-0770")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
